who: Frank Robert Chalk, historian of genocide and international relations at Concordia University, PhD Wisconsin 1970.

evidence.says: Concordia identifies Frank Chalk as professor of history, with a Wisconsin PhD and research on genocide, Africa and foreign policy.

The Frank Robert Chalk authority explicitly cites Concordia's faculty profile, his Wisconsin degrees and his 1970 doctoral thesis, The United States and the International Struggle for Rubber, 1914-1941.
Christopher John Young's thesis approval page names Dr. F. Chalk as thesis co-supervisor and gives an approval date of December 13, 2019.

notes: The authority directly links the full name to the university and doctorate. The other candidate's authority concerns It's Your Time You're Wasting.

who: Alfred D. Chandler Jr., business historian at Johns Hopkins during 1963-1970 and subsequently Harvard Business School, PhD Harvard 1952.

evidence.says: Harvard identifies the business historian as Alfred Chandler Jr.; he earned his PhD in 1952, joined Johns Hopkins in 1963 and moved to Harvard Business School in 1970.
The similarly named Alfred D. (Alfred Dupont) candidate is the author of Local Self-Government (1908), an earlier individual.
The Alfred D. Chandler III authority is based on a field-producer credit for Different Drummers: Daring to Make Peace in the Mideast (2003).
Harvard's finding aid identifies Alfred D. Chandler Jr., the business-history professor, and Alfred Dupont Chandler III as separate people.

notes: None of the supplied candidates is Alfred D. Chandler Jr. The remaining authorities have different given names or identify medical, engineering, fiction or earlier authors.

who: Diane Shaver Clemens, US diplomatic historian at UC Berkeley, PhD UC Santa Barbara 1966.

evidence.says: The university memorial identifies Diane Shaver Clemens as a Berkeley history professor from 1972 until retirement in 2006, with a 1966 Santa Barbara PhD on the Yalta Conference.
The Diane Shaver Clemens authority records the variants Diane Clemens and Diane S. Clemens and cites Berkeley's 1992/93 directory and From Isolationism to Internationalism (1993).

notes: The authority's Berkeley affiliation and diplomatic-history work agree with the supervisor's institution, period and doctorate.

who: Howard Francis Cline, historian of Latin America, Yale faculty 1947-1949, PhD Harvard 1947.

evidence.says: The scholarly memorial in Indiana 1 (1973), pp. 237-241, states that Cline completed a Harvard doctorate in 1947 on nineteenth-century Yucatan and taught history at Yale in 1947-1949.

The Howard Francis Cline authority also records Howard F. Cline, identifies a historian of Latin America and director of the Library of Congress Hispanic Foundation, and lists Mexico, Revolution to Evolution, 1940-1960.

notes: The full name, field, Harvard doctorate and Yale appointment immediately before Gibson's 1950 degree support the match.

who: Cheryll Ann Cody, historian of slavery at the University of Houston, PhD Minnesota 1982.

evidence.says: The June 1987 American Historical Review contributor biography identifies Cheryll Ann Cody as an assistant professor of history at Houston with a Minnesota PhD and research on the Ball plantation communities.
The library catalogue lists Cody's Slave Demography and Family Formation: A Community Study of the Ball Family Plantations, 1720-1896 as a Minnesota PhD dissertation, 1982.
The Cheryll Ann Cody authority is based on Slave Demography and Family Formation (1982), the same dissertation.

notes: The candidate's dissertation matches the supervisor's doctorate, and the publisher biography independently establishes the Houston appointment.

who: Elizabeth Cometti, historian of early America and West Virginia at West Virginia University, PhD Virginia 1939.

evidence.says: The university finding aid identifies Elizabeth Cometti as a West Virginia University history professor and a member of John William Larner's dissertation panel.
The library catalogue lists Cometti's The Departments of the Quartermaster and Clothier-General, 1775-1780 as a University of Virginia PhD dissertation, 1939.
The Elizabeth Cometti authority cites The Thirty-Fifth State (1966) and Jefferson's Ideas on a University Library.
In an interview, Ferling describes his graduate work at West Virginia University in the 1960s and names Elizabeth Cometti, an early-America specialist, as his mentor.

notes: The authority's historical works, exact doctorate and independently documented WVU mentoring identify the same historian.

who: Sandi E. Cooper, historian of European peace movements and women at the CUNY Graduate Center and College of Staten Island, PhD NYU.

evidence.says: Irene Meisel's 2016 history dissertation record explicitly names Sandi E. Cooper as advisor.
CUNY identifies Sandi E. Cooper as professor of history and women's and gender studies with an NYU PhD; her publications include Patriotic Pacifism.
The Sandi E. Cooper authority cites Patriotic Pacifism and records that exact author name.

notes: The student's repository record supplies a direct supervisor-name bridge. The separate Sandi Cooper authority n83011833 concerns Soups & Salads.

who: Sarah Cornell, historian of the Civil War era, slavery and US-Mexican relations at UMass Amherst, PhD NYU.

evidence.says: UMass identifies Cornell as a history lecturer specializing in the Civil War era, the US South and borderlands, previously at New Mexico; her work includes Citizens of Nowhere.
The 2008-2009 New Mexico catalogue lists Sarah Cornell as a history assistant professor with an NYU PhD.
This Sarah Cornell authority identifies a Stockholm Resilience Centre scholar associated with The Planet in 2050 and Understanding the Earth System.
The other Sarah Cornell authority identifies the translator of Cixous's Three Steps on the Ladder of Writing (1993).

The repository thesis Translation and Travelling Theory, printed p. 139, identifies the Cixous translator as a member of the Centre d'études féminines since 1976 whose doctoral thesis there concerned Cixous.

notes: The same-name candidates concern Earth-system research and Cixous translation, with different doctoral fields. The remaining candidates concern nineteenth-century individuals or Sara Cornell's art-history textbook; none identifies the UMass historian.
